To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

dietary energy restriction and insulin resistance exert adverse effects on cognitive function, and that these adverse effects are associated with the down-regulation of neuroprotective genes and the up-regulation genes that encode proteins involved in cell death.

excessive caloric intake and/or insulin resistance are risk factors for age-related cognitive dysfunction and disease and that dietary energy restriction and/or drugs that activate adaptive cellular stress response mechanisms are effective approaches for preserving cognition in rodents and may be useful in the treatment and/or prevention of human cognitive dysfunction.

1) dietary energy restriction can prevent and/or ameliorate the cognitive dysfunction associated with aging and Alzheimer’s disease in rodent models, 2) dietary energy restriction and other approaches that enhance insulin sensitivity can improve cognitive function in humans, 3) dietary energy restriction, insulin-sensitization and the activation of adaptive cellular stress response mechanisms can improve cognition by promoting neural plasticity and neuroprotection, and 4) alternate day calorie restriction, neurotrophins, glucagon-like
In summary, our research is concerned with

understanding the mechanisms by which energy balance and insulin resistance influence brain aging and cognitive function, and with translating these findings into strategies that will improve the health of the aging brain.
the identification of molecular mechanisms by which energy balance and energy metabolism regulate neural plasticity and cognitive function in aging.
understanding the mechanisms underlying the adverse effects of insulin resistance and obesity on brain aging and the means for preventing or reversing them.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the impact of dietary energy intake on cognitive aging is a complex process and that more studies are necessary to fully understand the mechanisms involved.
dietary energy restriction is the best approach to preserve cognitive function in aging.

a healthy diet is essential for healthy aging and that dietary energy intake and energy balance are important factors to consider in the design of interventions to preserve cognitive function in aging.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a reduction in energy intake, and an increase in energy expenditure, can improve brain function in rodents.

dietary energy restriction and insulin resistance can affect cognitive aging and that these factors may interact to influence the brain's ability to maintain its plasticity and to resist the effects of disease.

a reduction in dietary energy intake can enhance neural plastic processes, improve cognition, and reduce the risk of neurodegenerative disease in rodents and may be a promising approach for preserving cognitive function in humans as they age.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dietary energy intake and the resulting state of energy balance are important determinants of cognitive health.
the brain has a remarkable capacity to adapt and repair itself in response to dietary energy restriction.
a diet that promotes energy homeostasis may help to preserve cognitive function during aging.
